subject: economics
intro: Economics leads to paid work analysing how resources, money and incentives move — forecasting and policy analysis, pricing risk, reading markets, and turning data into decisions for firms and governments.

roles.title: Economists
roles.what: Conduct research, prepare reports and formulate plans to address economic problems related to the production and distribution of goods and services, or to monetary and fiscal policy — collecting and processing the data behind the advice.
roles.where: The government-and-macroeconomy unit — fiscal policy, monetary policy, economic growth and unemployment — is literally the subject matter economists analyse, while the basic economic problem and PPC diagrams start the modelling habit the job is built on.

roles.title: Actuaries
roles.what: Analyse statistical data on mortality, accident, sickness, disability and retirement rates to build probability tables that forecast risk and future liabilities, pricing insurance and pension promises so they can actually be paid.
roles.where: The syllabus's demand, supply and price-determination topics explain how insurance markets price; the living-standards and poverty topics in the development unit connect to the demographic and social data actuaries quantify.

roles.title: Statisticians
roles.what: Develop and apply mathematical and statistical theory to collect, organise, interpret and summarise numerical data — designing samples, testing models and turning raw numbers into information others can act on.
roles.where: Elasticity calculations, index numbers for living standards and the cost-revenue analysis of firms train exactly the habit of summarising data into a usable measure that statistical work demands.

roles.title: Market Research Analysts and Marketing Specialists
roles.what: Research conditions in local, regional, national or online markets, gathering information to estimate potential sales of a product or service or to plan marketing and advertising campaigns.
roles.where: The allocation-of-resources unit — demand curves, price changes and elasticity of demand — is the daily toolkit for gauging what customers will buy; firms' costs, revenue and objectives supply the business side.

roles.title: Economics Teachers, Postsecondary
roles.what: Teach economics courses at colleges and universities — lecturing on micro- and macroeconomic theory, econometrics and policy, marking student work, and often researching and publishing alongside teaching.
roles.where: The syllabus units on markets, macroeconomic intervention and economic development are the foundations these teachers unpack in first-year principles courses — the same diagrams, from PPC to AD/AS, at greater depth.
